name: Acrobat
description:
The gap is wider than it looks, but you've got to make it anyway. You run forward, spacing your steps carefully - one, two, three - then you anchor your pole against the lip of the roof, tighten your grip and spring upward, propelled high over the busy alleyway below. As you complete an elegant arc downward you see the captain turn, noticing you, but too late. Using the momentum of your fall, you bring your pole down squarely on the crown of his helmet with a satisfying clang. He goes down. His guards wheel around to come to his defense, but you use the rebound of the initial blow to your advantage, bringing your pole down and around you in a wide sweep, knocking the legs out from under all five of them. You leap over the tangle of bodies and make a beeline for the doorway that leads down into the chamber where the prince is being held hostage. By the time the guards manage to get back to their feet, you're already gone.

Acrobats can run further, jump higher, climb faster and get to more places than anyone else. They aren't the hardest hitters on the battlefield, but they are incredibly difficult to pin down - leaping into and out of melee range before their opponents can react.

Play an Acrobat if you want to:

  • Use movement itself as a resource, turning raw speed and agility into actions, attacks, and advantages that others simply cannot replicate.

  • Go where no one else can, scaling, vaulting, and threading through environments with a ease that makes the impossible look routine.

  • Fight with unconventional weapons and techniques, from a long pole to coiled chain to precisely targeted strikes that disable a foe's body piece by piece.

Questions to consider when making an Acrobat:

  • Where did they train? A traveling circus, a martial arts tradition, a life spent free-running across urban rooftops, or simple feral necessity?

  • What weapon—or fighting style—feels most like an extension of who they are? Is there a philosophy behind the choice, or is it purely practical?

  • How do they feel about their own physical capability? Is it a source of pride and identity, or simply a tool they use without much reflection?

  • Are they a performer as well as a fighter? Does anyone know what they can do, or do they keep it in reserve?

  • What is a place they have reached that no one thought reachable—and what did they find there?
